rationale:
PINS the Kotlin 2.2 CONTEXT-PARAMETER guard. `context(session: FirSession)` written above a declaration has no node in tree-sitter-kotlin: the header parses as a top-level call_expression whose callee is the soft keyword `context`, with an ERROR node standing in for each `: Type`. Before the guard the analyzer published `calls[Global -> context]` at 0.7 for every header — a DECLARATION stored as a CALL, sourced to a symbol no kotlin file declares. MEASURED on a 400-file stratified draw of bb_tests/repositories/kotlin@9b80c8ff: 20 headers in 4 files; 28 of that sample's 524 `Global` call edges.

The pins cover the four ways this guard can be wrong, because the over-corrections are all plausible and all different defects: (1) the header yields NO call edge at all; (2) the declaration UNDER the header keeps its own edges — a context parameter does not swallow the function written below it, and the call inside it is sourced to that function; (3) a REAL call to a user-declared function named `context` is still a call, because `context` is only a keyword in the header POSITION — `fun context(x: Int)` is a legal declaration; (4) the same holds for a header above a CLASS and above a PROPERTY, so the guard is not accidentally specific to functions.

`normalizeName` is not a stdlib leaf, so the pins are about attribution and not about the stdlib filter.

expectRelationships.note: the declaration UNDER a context header keeps its own call edge, sourced to itself. A guard that dropped the header's whole subtree would lose this.
a header above a CLASS does not swallow the class's methods
a header above a PROPERTY: the top-level property owns its own initializer's call
`context` is a SOFT keyword. A program may declare and call a function of that name, and the guard keys on the ERROR inside the argument list, not on the name — so this real call survives.
a context parameter does not make the declaration non-exportable

and it must not be attributed to the package either
